30.bp: A recommender is a gatekeeper for attention. A shop, video site, or news feed may hold millions of possible items, but a person only sees a short row or page. The practical question is therefore not whether the system can assign a decent score to every item somewhere in the catalog. The question is whether the few items placed in front of this user are the ones most likely to match that user's current taste. Talos serves that narrow but central decision. The abstract says recommender systems care especially about Top-K accuracy, such as precision and recall among the first K shown results. That is the part users experience and the part businesses act on. The paper tries to train the recommender so its learning target matches this visible short-list goal, instead of spending effort on correctness across the entire item set, much of which will never be shown.
30.wh: The hard part is that Top-K quality depends on position, not just on raw scores. To know whether an item belongs in the first K, the system normally has to compare it against many other items and determine where it sits in the ordered list. That ranking step is expensive when the catalog is large and must be repeated during training. It also creates an awkward learning target: a tiny score change can move an item across the K boundary, while the usual training machinery prefers smoother feedback. The abstract adds another pressure: user preferences and recorded data can change or be biased, so a score pattern learned from yesterday's behavior may not match today's audience. The central tension is accuracy near the visible boundary versus the cost and instability of repeatedly sorting a huge pile of candidates.
30.naive: A smart beginner would train the recommender to give liked items higher scores than unliked items, then sort all items and check whether the best ones land in the top K. That sounds faithful to the user-facing goal because it uses the actual ordered list. It fails on cost and learning clarity. Sorting every candidate during training is heavy, and the model receives a difficult signal because membership in the top K changes abruptly. Another beginner shortcut would optimize average score quality over all items, but that wastes effort on the long tail of items that will never be displayed and may neglect mistakes right at the cutoff where shown and hidden items trade places.
30.ap: Talos changes the training question from, "What is this item's exact rank among all items?" to, "Is this item's score above the score level that marks the top K region?" The abstract says it uses a quantile technique: a quantile is a boundary value in an ordered pile, such as the score that separates the highest few percent from the rest. Instead of repeatedly computing full ranking positions, Talos learns score thresholds that stand in for the Top-K cutoff. Items are then judged by simpler comparisons against those thresholds. The paper also estimates the thresholds through sampling, so it does not need to inspect the full catalog each time. A constraint term prevents the model from winning by inflating all scores, and a smooth stand-in function makes the abrupt cutoff easier to learn from.
30.mech: The mechanism begins with users, candidate items, and predicted preference scores produced by a recommender. The ordinary Top-K route would sort many candidate scores for each user and measure whether the relevant items appear among the first K. Talos replaces that expensive sort with learned score thresholds. First, it treats the top of the score list as a boundary problem: if the Kth best score for a user or training group were known, then an item above that boundary would count like a top-list item and one below would not. Second, because computing that boundary exactly is costly, the method estimates it from samples. The sampling-based regression algorithm learns to predict thresholds accurately enough to guide training without ranking every item. Third, the loss function compares predicted item scores with these learned thresholds, turning ranking-dependent operations into score-versus-boundary checks. Fourth, the training process includes a constraint against score inflation. Without that guard, the model might push scores upward broadly rather than learning sharper separation near the top. Fifth, the abstract says Talos uses a tailored smooth stand-in for the discontinuous top-K decision, so small score changes produce usable training feedback. The output is a recommender whose training pressure is aimed at improving the visible top K list.
30.math: The main mathematical idea is ranking by thresholds. Ranking means turning many candidate items into an order by assigning scores and comparing them. Top-K accuracy cares mainly about whether useful items cross the visibility boundary. A quantile is the score value at a chosen position in an ordered set; here it acts like a learned fence between likely top-K items and the rest. This matters because finding the exact rank of every item is costly, while comparing one score with one boundary is much cheaper. The second idea is sampling: a smaller chosen subset stands in for the huge item pile, so long as it gives a good estimate of the boundary. The third idea is regression, which means learning to predict a number, in this case the threshold score, from observed examples. The fourth idea is a loss function, a rule that says what counts as wrong during training. Talos defines wrongness around top-K placement rather than around all-item score quality. The fifth idea is a smooth surrogate, a learnable substitute for a hard yes-or-no cutoff. The tradeoff is accuracy at the recommendation boundary versus computation, with an added stability tradeoff because scores must separate items without simply growing everywhere.
30.dots: This paper sits in the recommender-systems family because it addresses the shared pressure of choosing a small useful set from a huge, changing pile. In the repo's recommender family notes, Talos is grouped with methods that repair the short-listing step before recommendation happens: the common failure is not knowing how to compare enough candidates cheaply and faithfully. It also connects to the ranking concept. Like search, retrieval, and risk triage papers, it turns many weak signs into an order, but it focuses on the boundary where an item becomes visible. It connects to the optimization concept because the paper defines a specific kind of wrongness, Top-K error, and trains the model to reduce that wrongness under cost and stability constraints. Probability enters through sampling: Talos trusts a partial view of the item pile to estimate a threshold that would otherwise require broader inspection.
30.ww: The approach should help because it aligns the learning signal with the decision users actually experience. If a recommender is judged by the first K items, then training it on average quality across all scores can spend too much effort far from the visible boundary. Talos concentrates pressure near that boundary by asking whether relevant items rise above learned top-K thresholds. This is a more direct lesson for the model: push the right items across the display line and keep less useful items below it. It is also cheaper because threshold comparison avoids repeated full ranking operations. The sampling step works when the sampled items preserve enough information about the score distribution to estimate the cutoff. The constraint against score inflation matters because a threshold method could otherwise be gamed by raising scores indiscriminately. The smooth stand-in for the hard cutoff supplies steadier feedback, which is especially useful when preferences or data biases shift and brittle boundary decisions would make training noisy.
30.po: The payoff is a recommender training objective aimed directly at Top-K accuracy, the part of recommendation that determines what a user sees. The abstract claims Talos improves effectiveness and efficiency by replacing ranking-position calculations with threshold comparisons, and it reports theoretical analysis plus empirical experiments for effectiveness, convergence, and resilience to changing data patterns. In practical terms, the promise is a system that spends less training effort sorting the entire catalog and more effort improving the few-item list that matters. It also gives the training process safeguards: threshold estimation for cost, a constraint for stable scores, and a smoother learning signal for abrupt top-K decisions.
30.limits: The abstract does not show the exact theorem statements, datasets, or failure cases, so the strength of the evidence cannot be judged from this input alone. Talos depends on learned thresholds being accurate enough to stand in for real top-K boundaries; poor samples or unusual score shapes could misplace that boundary. The method also assumes predicted scores are meaningful and comparable, and that preventing score inflation is enough to keep training stable. Changing user preferences and biased records are addressed by the proposed smooth surrogate, but the abstract does not prove that every real platform shift will be handled. It also does not establish long-term user welfare, fairness, diversity, or business effects beyond top-K accuracy.

31.bp: A blockchain is a shared ledger that many computers agree to maintain without one central owner. Its trust depends on digital signatures, public records, and agreement rules: a user proves control of an account, validators accept the proof, and everyone can later check the history. This tutorial starts from a coming pressure on that trust. Quantum computers use physical behavior at very small scales to solve some mathematical puzzles in a different way from ordinary computers. The abstract says those advances threaten the public-key algorithms that protect blockchain systems, digital signatures, and distributed agreement. The practical question is therefore not only how to make faster computation. It is how a web system that stores value, identity, provenance, and shared data standards can remain trustworthy when one of its old locks may stop being strong. The session serves builders who need a roadmap from laboratory quantum ideas to usable blockchain security, privacy, governance, and interoperable data infrastructure.
31.wh: The hard part is that blockchain security is public by design. Transactions, public keys, signatures, and agreement messages are meant to be copied and checked by many parties. That openness helps auditability, but it also gives future attackers a long-lived record to study. If a classical public-key puzzle becomes easy for a strong quantum machine, old evidence that once looked safe can become a source of private-key exposure or forged signatures. A second difficulty is translation. The abstract says the move from theoretical quantum breakthroughs to real blockchain applications remains limited. Knowing that quantum computing matters is not enough; builders must choose post-quantum cryptography, consider quantum-assisted techniques, preserve efficiency, fit decentralized agreement, and keep privacy and ethical data governance in view. The problem spans physics, cryptography, economics, human-computer interaction, and standards. A narrow patch can fail because it protects one lock while ignoring the way people, validators, applications, and data formats actually share trust.
31.naive: A smart beginner might say: wait until quantum computers are powerful enough, then replace the signature scheme. That fails because blockchains preserve old public data, and migration takes time across wallets, validators, exchanges, applications, and standards. Another beginner answer is to encrypt more things. That misses the specific failure: signatures and public-key identity are not just hidden messages; they are public proofs that let strangers verify ownership and agreement. A third shortcut is to pick any advertised quantum-safe algorithm and drop it in. The abstract warns against that by framing the tutorial around efficiency, scalable architectures, privacy, human use, ethical governance, and open standards. A cryptographic component that is mathematically promising but too heavy, hard to use, poorly standardized, or misfit to consensus can make the web system less trustworthy rather than more secure.
31.ap: The central move is educational and architectural rather than a single new algorithm. The tutorial puts three worlds in one room: quantum computing, blockchain applications, and data standards. First it rebuilds the principles of quantum computing so participants can understand why certain old public-key protections are exposed. Then it maps the defense space: post-quantum cryptography, meaning new public-key locks built from problems not known to fall quickly to quantum machines, and quantum-assisted cryptography, meaning security mechanisms that use quantum behavior itself where useful. It also treats quantum techniques as possible aids for efficiency, randomness, and resilience in decentralized systems, not only as threats. The cooperative part matters: trustworthy web infrastructure is not only code. It needs shared standards, privacy boundaries, human-centered design, economic incentives, and reproducible ways to compare systems. The Amazon Braket component turns the idea from distant theory into hands-on comparison across cloud quantum backends.
31.mech: The mechanism begins with the existing blockchain stack. The inputs are public keys, digital signatures, transaction records, distributed consensus messages, privacy requirements, application needs, and data standards. The tutorial first asks what each part is doing. A signature proves that an account holder authorized an action. Consensus lets many machines agree on the same ledger state. Standards make data understandable across tools and organizations. Then quantum computing is introduced as a new kind of machine whose operating rules change which mathematical puzzles are costly to solve. That threat is compared against the current cryptographic foundations, especially public-key algorithms. The next step is substitution and augmentation. Post-quantum schemes are candidates for replacing vulnerable locks, while quantum-assisted techniques may provide stronger randomness, communication security, or other support for decentralized operation. Efficiency is treated as a scoring pressure: a defense must not make validation, storage, or communication so expensive that the chain becomes unusable. Privacy and governance are added as constraints, because a secure ledger can still harm users if data exposure or authority rules are poorly designed. Finally, participants use Amazon Braket to interact with cloud quantum computation and compare multiple quantum backends. The output is not a deployed chain; it is a roadmap and shared mental model for building quantum-ready blockchain systems.
31.math: The main mathematical idea is one-way difficulty. A public-key system works when one direction is easy and the reverse direction is infeasible: it is easy to verify a signature with public information, but hard to recover the private secret or forge the signature. Quantum computing matters because it changes the cost of some reverse directions. The tutorial therefore has to separate old hardness assumptions from new ones. Post-quantum cryptography keeps the public-verification shape but chooses different underlying puzzles, aiming for problems where no efficient quantum attack is known. Quantum-assisted cryptography uses a different principle: some quantum states cannot be copied or measured without disturbance, so the act of spying can become physically visible in certain communication settings. Blockchain adds distributed agreement math. Many parties must converge on one ledger even though messages arrive separately and some participants may be strategic or faulty. Randomness matters because leader selection, sampling, and protocol choices often need unpredictability that attackers cannot steer. Data standards add another kind of structure: shared formats reduce ambiguity so evidence can be checked across systems. The tradeoff is security versus cost and interoperability versus local freedom.
31.dots: This paper sits beside the conference's privacy and security work because it asks what can safely cross a boundary. Federated-learning leakage papers ask whether shared updates reveal private training data; cookie-theft and side-channel papers ask whether ordinary web plumbing leaks secrets; zero-knowledge and verification papers ask how to prove a rule without exposing the private object. The quantum-safe blockchain tutorial brings the same boundary question to decentralized ledgers: which public evidence can remain public when future machines may read it differently? It also connects to misinformation and trust work. A blockchain often promises provenance, but provenance is only useful if signatures, standards, and governance remain credible. Finally, it touches systems and optimization ideas: defenses must save scarce time, storage, communication, and human coordination while raising security. The abstract's emphasis on interdisciplinary collaboration explains why this is a tutorial. The deeper problem is not one method; it is preparing a trust infrastructure before the threat fully arrives.
31.ww: The approach works as a tutorial because the failure mode is partly conceptual fragmentation. A blockchain engineer may know consensus but not quantum hardware. A quantum researcher may know the physics but not wallet migration, validator incentives, or open web standards. A policy or data-governance person may understand accountability but not why public-key assumptions are fragile. Putting the pieces together helps because the correct action depends on their interaction. Post-quantum cryptography addresses the direct lock-breaking risk. Quantum-assisted methods may strengthen randomness, communication, or resilience where the deployment setting supports them. Open standards make migration and comparison possible across organizations rather than leaving every chain to invent incompatible defenses. Hands-on cloud quantum experimentation helps participants see that quantum backends are real systems with different behavior, not magic boxes. The benefit over the naive approach is timing and integration: it encourages planned migration, efficiency testing, privacy review, and governance design before a crisis forces rushed replacements.
31.po: The payoff is a shared roadmap for a quantum-ready internet layer. The tutorial gives participants a way to reason about why quantum computing threatens blockchain security, which cryptographic directions are meant to resist that threat, and how quantum tools might also improve efficiency, randomness, and resilience. It grounds that roadmap in blockchain applications, privacy, human-computer interaction, ethical data governance, open standards, and reproducibility. The Amazon Braket component adds practical exposure by letting participants compare quantum backends. The result promised by the abstract is not a measured performance gain for one protocol, but a clearer path for building trustworthy decentralized web systems before classical cryptographic assumptions become unsafe.
31.limits: The abstract describes a cooperative tutorial, so it does not prove that a particular post-quantum scheme, quantum-assisted protocol, or blockchain architecture is best. It assumes the quantum threat is important enough to plan for now, but it does not give deployment timelines, migration costs, or attack thresholds. Cloud quantum demonstrations can teach principles, yet they are not evidence that production blockchain workloads can already rely on quantum hardware. Post-quantum choices still need standardization, implementation review, usability testing, and performance checks inside real consensus systems. The broader governance claims also require institutional adoption. A roadmap can align people, but it cannot by itself make wallets, validators, applications, and standards migrate correctly.

32.bp: This paper is about rebuilding a person's path when the usual supports for map software are weak or absent. In well-mapped cities, a noisy phone trace can be snapped back onto known roads. In remote, underserved, or disaster-like regions, that shortcut may not exist: roads may be missing from digital maps, GPS points may be sparse, and the recorded path may look like a few disconnected dots. The real-world need is practical movement understanding in places where infrastructure data is thin. A relief team, mobility analyst, or local service may still need to know how people moved between observed locations. The paper treats web crowdsourced location data as the substitute for an explicit road network. Instead of asking a map to say which route is legal, it asks historical traces to reveal the movement habits of the region itself, then uses those habits to recover missing parts of an individual trajectory.
32.wh: The difficulty is that a path is not just a set of points. The missing middle must be consistent with where the traveler was before, where they were later, and what movements are plausible in that place. When roads are known, they strongly constrain the answer: a car probably follows connected road segments rather than a straight line through obstacles. In the paper's setting, the road graph is unavailable or poorly mapped, so that constraint has to be inferred indirectly. GPS scarcity adds a second problem because the visible points may be far apart or unreliable. Cross-region transfer is also hard: movement patterns learned from one region may not fit an unseen region with different geography, density, or informal routes. The system must therefore borrow structure from scarce historical data without simply memorizing one area and forcing that shape onto another.
32.naive: A smart beginner might draw a straight line between the last reliable location and the next reliable location, or smooth the observed GPS points until the path looks less jagged. That fails because real movement is constrained by paths, terrain, settlements, and local habits that a straight line does not know. Another simple answer is to use a standard road map or a model trained in mapped cities. That fails in the intended setting because the road network may be missing and the new region may not resemble the training region. A third shortcut is to use only nearby historical traces. But if the area is underserved, there may be too few examples at exactly the right place and scale.
32.ap: The core idea is to build an implicit map from movement records themselves. RHTR divides a region into grids at multiple sizes. A coarse grid keeps broad direction and displacement patterns, such as how movement tends to flow across larger parts of the area. A fine grid keeps more local detail around observed points. The paper calls these grid-based offset maps: each grid cell stores learned hints about likely movement offsets, meaning how positions tend to shift from one part of a trajectory to another. These maps are not drawn roads, but they play a similar constraining role. When a trajectory has gaps, the model samples information around the observed points, forms region-aware encodings, meaning compact descriptions tied to that local area, and reconstructs the missing segment from coarse to fine. It first chooses a broad plausible shape, then refines local positions.
32.mech: The mechanism starts with historical location data collected from web crowdsourcing and a damaged or incomplete trajectory that needs recovery. First, the region is overlaid with grids at several resolutions. At the coarsest level, each cell summarizes broad movement tendencies from the historical traces. At finer levels, smaller cells record more detailed offset information near particular places. The important transformation is from raw point histories into maps of likely displacement: given a place and surrounding context, what nearby movement directions and sizes have appeared before? Next, for the trajectory being repaired, the model looks around its observed points and samples these grid maps. This sampling turns a global regional memory into local clues for the specific path. The resulting region-aware descriptions are ordered as a sequence, because the path must respect before-and-after structure. Then the recovery process works from coarse to fine. It first uses wider contextual information to sketch the missing segment at a rough scale, reducing the huge set of possible paths to a smaller plausible zone. It then uses finer grid information to sharpen local details. The output is a reconstructed trajectory: a sequence of inferred locations that fills the missing parts while staying consistent with the observed endpoints and with movement patterns learned from the region.
32.math: The main mathematical object is a sequence of locations, where order matters because each point limits what the next point can sensibly be. A second object is a grid, which turns continuous geography into countable cells so the model can store and compare movement evidence. The offset map is a learned table of displacements: instead of storing only where people were, it stores how positions tend to move from one place toward another. That is a way of estimating hidden movement structure from repeated observations. Probability is present in the everyday sense of weighing plausible paths more heavily when similar movements have appeared in the historical data. Similarity also matters: evidence from one nearby cell can help another only if the cells share movement behavior. The hierarchical part is a scale tradeoff. Coarse cells give stable regional patterns but blur local detail; fine cells give detail but may be sparse and noisy. The coarse-to-fine process uses the stable large-scale guess to guide the detailed local guess. Learning from examples enters by adjusting internal settings so recovered paths better match known trajectories in training data. The tradeoff is accuracy versus available evidence: use too much coarse structure and the path is vague; trust fine local data too much and scarcity can mislead.
32.dots: This paper connects to the conference's sequence work because a trajectory is an ordered record, not a pile of coordinates. Like forecasting and memory papers, it asks which past and nearby evidence should still matter at the next step. It also sits inside spatiotemporal reasoning: the answer depends on both location and order in time, with missing stretches that must be repaired rather than merely predicted as one number. It is close to graph reasoning, but with an important twist. Many graph methods would rely on explicit nodes and links such as road intersections and road segments. Here those links are missing, so the model has to infer a softer movement structure from crowdsourced traces and grids. It also echoes low-resource and transfer problems elsewhere in the data, where systems must serve underserved settings by borrowing evidence without assuming that richer, cleaner regions fully describe the target region.
32.ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because it replaces an empty map with evidence about how people actually moved. A straight line ignores local movement habits; a road-based method may have no roads to use; a model copied from another region may carry the wrong assumptions. RHTR gives the recovery process a middle ground. Coarse grids make the model less brittle when data is scarce, because broad movement tendencies can be learned from fewer examples than exact local paths. Fine grids add detail where enough local evidence exists. Sampling around observed points matters because the same missing distance can mean different things in different parts of a region. The sequential representation matters because the missing locations are not independent guesses; each inferred point should make sense between the previous and next parts of the trajectory. The coarse-to-fine mechanism works like narrowing a search: first rule out implausible large shapes, then spend detail where it is most useful. That structure fits roadless recovery because the method learns constraints from movement traces instead of requiring them to be supplied as roads.
32.po: The payoff is better trajectory recovery in places where ordinary map matching is weakest: remote or underserved regions, sparse GPS settings, and disaster-like scenarios with missing spatial information. The abstract says experiments on two public datasets simulate these conditions, including transfer across regions, and report state-of-the-art recovery performance. In practical terms, the paper buys the ability to infer missing route segments from web crowdsourced movement evidence even when explicit road networks are unavailable. That makes location inference less dependent on already well-mapped infrastructure and more useful for areas whose digital maps and GPS traces are incomplete.
32.limits: The method assumes historical crowdsourced location data contains enough repeated movement behavior to reveal useful regional structure. If a place has almost no traces, or if movement changes sharply after a disaster, the learned offset maps may describe the wrong world. Grid cells also impose boundaries: coarse cells can hide important local constraints, while fine cells can become sparse. The abstract reports two public datasets that simulate underserved and disaster-like settings, but it does not prove reliability for every region, travel mode, terrain, privacy condition, or real emergency. It also does not specify how errors in crowdsourced data affect recovery.

33.bp: This paper is about who gets to participate when a decentralized finance protocol rewards people according to how much money they control. Decentralized finance, or DeFi, means financial software running on a blockchain rather than through a bank. In the setting described here, the protocol is ranking-dependent: accounts or brokers with larger fund balances sit higher in the ranking and receive better revenue opportunities. That creates a practical barrier before any fancy market theory appears. A small stakeholder may be willing to participate, but their small balance puts them in a losing position from the start. LiquidityPool is proposed as a collective participation tool: many smaller stakeholders combine funds so the group can act with the scale that the protocol rewards. The paper asks a difficult market-design question: in this kind of ranking-based DeFi world, is breaking power into many competitors actually better, or can aggregation make the system more accessible and more socially useful?
33.wh: The hard part is that the ranking rule changes the shape of competition. In a normal beginner picture of a market, more competitors should push outcomes toward better prices or better service, while one dominant actor should look suspicious. The abstract says that picture can fail here because revenue grows in a curved way with fund size: bigger pools do not merely earn proportionally more, they can gain extra advantage from scale. Once that is true, a small initial difference can feed on itself. A broker with more funds earns more, the higher earnings strengthen the broker's position, and the gap becomes harder to close. The paper calls the balanced many-party outcome knife-edge, meaning it exists only under unusually exact starting conditions. If early asymmetry crosses a critical threshold, the system tends toward one dominant pool no matter where it began. So the difficulty is not only unfair access; it is self-reinforcing market structure.
33.naive: A smart beginner would try to protect small stakeholders by encouraging many separate brokers or pools to compete. The hope would be simple: if no one becomes too large, smaller participants have more choices and no single actor can dominate. That fails if the protocol pays higher-ranked, larger-balance actors in a way that creates economies of scale. Fragmenting funds may leave every small pool below the useful participation line, while one aggregated pool can reach the rank where revenue is available. Another naive answer is to tell small stakeholders to participate individually. But the abstract says higher fund balances achieve better revenue performance, so individual small accounts begin with a structural disadvantage rather than a temporary inconvenience.
33.ap: The paper's central move is to treat pooling as an economic mechanism rather than merely a convenience. LiquidityPool gathers resources from multiple stakeholders so they can participate as a larger fund in protocols where rank matters. The analysis then asks what strategic actors would do around such pools. It uses a multi-leader multi-follower Stackelberg competition: in plain terms, some actors move first, others respond, and everyone tries to choose the action that improves their own revenue while anticipating what the rest will do. This lets the authors compare fragmented competition with concentration under the actual ranking-dependent revenue shape. The surprising claim is that the concentrated outcome can produce higher social welfare than many smaller competitors, because the revenue rule rewards aggregation. The protocol is therefore not just a way to make one pool bigger; it is a way to let small stakeholders cross a participation barrier created by rank-based DeFi design.
33.mech: The mechanism starts with stakeholders who each control some amount of funds and a DeFi protocol whose revenue opportunities depend on fund-size ranking. The first input is the distribution of balances: some brokers or stakeholders have more money than others. The second input is the protocol's revenue rule, especially the fact that larger fund balances receive better revenue performance. LiquidityPool then changes the unit of participation. Instead of each small stakeholder entering separately, their funds are aggregated into a collective pool, so the protocol sees a larger participant capable of competing at a higher rank. The game-theoretic part asks how multiple leaders and followers behave when they can choose or respond to such market positions. A leader's decision affects the follower's best response, and one party's fund size affects the rankings faced by everyone else. The analysis looks for stable outcomes, where no actor has a reason to move away given the others' choices. It finds that symmetric multi-party competition is fragile: it survives only under restrictive initial conditions. Once starting balances are unequal beyond a critical level, the process converges toward monopolistic concentration. The experiments then check this pattern using real Ethereum blockchain data across different market structures. The output is a claim about both structure and access: concentration appears repeatedly, welfare gains are modest, and 98% of small-volume stakeholders become able to participate.
33.math: The main mathematical idea is strategic response. Game theory, in everyday terms, studies settings where one person's best move depends on what others are expected to do. Here the people or brokers are not isolated; each fund decision affects rank, and rank affects revenue. Stackelberg competition adds order to that interaction: leaders choose first, followers observe or respond, and everyone reasons through the chain rather than treating the market as a crowd of identical independent actors. The second idea is equilibrium, a resting pattern where each participant's choice makes sense given the others' choices. The paper's knife-edge result says the equal, many-party resting pattern is mathematically delicate, not broadly stable. The third idea is a threshold: a line in the starting asymmetry such that crossing it changes the long-run structure. Below it, balanced competition may be possible under special conditions; above it, concentration takes over. The fourth idea is a convex revenue function, meaning the reward curve bends upward so added funds can bring more than proportional benefit. That curve creates economies of scale. The tradeoff is competition versus access: fragmentation may reduce concentration, but it can also strand small stakeholders below the rank needed to earn.
33.dots: This paper connects directly to the conference's ranking idea, but in an unusual direction. Many ranking papers ask how to sort documents, products, answers, or candidates so a user sees the best few. Here ranking is not just a display order; it changes who gets paid. That makes rank a market force. It also connects to matching and allocation, because the practical question is how scarce opportunity is assigned among stakeholders with different fund sizes. A local concept note says matching breaks when the act of matching changes the world; this paper is an example because pooling changes the ranks that determine later revenue. It also sits beside other repo blockchain and DeFi records, including atomic arbitrage, blockchain scheduling, laundering behavior, and Ethereum network security. Those neighboring papers share a pressure: decentralized systems look open, but their rules, timing, topology, or incentives can still create strong advantages for some actors.
33.ww: The approach works, according to the abstract, because it models the actual feedback loop instead of importing a market intuition from a different setting. Classical competition stories often assume that splitting a market among more actors disciplines prices or output. In this DeFi setting, the revenue rule rewards rank and scale, so splitting funds can destroy the very capacity needed to participate effectively. Pooling works when the combined balance lifts small stakeholders into a rank where revenue opportunities are reachable. The game model helps because it treats each broker's balance as part of everyone else's environment: one actor's aggregation changes the ranking landscape for the rest. The threshold result explains why small early differences can become large structural outcomes. If the revenue curve bends upward, a larger actor gains an advantage that can reinforce further concentration. That is why monopolistic concentration can show higher welfare than fragmented competition here. It is not because monopoly is generally good; it is because this protocol's payoff rule can make scale socially useful for access.
33.po: The payoff is a clearer way to reason about DeFi systems where rank determines revenue. LiquidityPool gives small-volume stakeholders a route into protocols that were previously inaccessible, and the abstract reports that 98% of such stakeholders can participate through the pooled design. The paper also gives a warning for policy and protocol design: traditional antitrust instincts that favor fragmentation may not fit ranking-dependent DeFi networks. The experiments on real Ethereum blockchain data support the theoretical pattern of monopolization across market structures. The welfare gains are described as modest, but the accessibility gain is substantial.
33.limits: The claim depends on the protocol really having ranking-dependent revenue and an upward-bending revenue curve that rewards scale. If another DeFi system pays roughly in proportion to funds, the argument for concentration would be weaker. The abstract does not give the full mechanism details for governance, fees, withdrawals, trust inside the pool, or how small stakeholders are protected from the pool operator. It also says welfare improvements are modest because wealth is already concentrated. The Ethereum validation supports the pattern, but the abstract does not prove that every chain, market period, or ranking rule will converge the same way.

34.bp: BeeQoS is about a shared cloud network where many applications are trying to use the same pipes at the same time. Some traffic belongs to interactive web services, mobile workloads, or web-of-things workloads where delay is visible to a person or device. Other traffic may be less urgent. The practical need is not simply to move as many bytes as possible; it is to make sure higher-priority flows get enough bandwidth and low delay while the cluster is busy and changing. In a Kubernetes cloud, applications appear, disappear, and shift their demand, so a rule written once can quickly become wrong. BeeQoS serves the operator who wants priority-aware bandwidth promises across many tenants without hand-tuning every machine. Its central claim is that quality of service should become a cloud-native control problem: fast packet handling close to the network path, live sensing of demand, and policy expression that fits cluster deployment.
34.wh: The hard part is that bandwidth is both shared and time-sensitive. A network link can be full even when every application looks reasonable on its own, because their peaks collide. If a high-priority service suddenly needs more capacity, the system must react before users see latency, but it cannot spend too much time making the decision. The abstract names two existing failure modes. Linux Traffic Control Hierarchical Token Bucket is static and unscalable: it can shape traffic, but its fixed hierarchy does not naturally follow many changing cloud flows. Cilium is cloud-native, but the abstract says it offers only coarse-grained rate limiting, which is too blunt when different flows have different priority and demand. The tension is speed versus control. Packet decisions must be extremely fast, yet the allocation rule must know enough about current demand to move capacity where it is needed.
34.naive: A smart beginner would divide the link into fixed slices: high-priority traffic gets a large slice, medium gets a smaller slice, and low gets whatever remains. That is easy to explain and easy to configure. It fails because real cloud demand is not fixed. A high-priority service may be quiet for a while, leaving reserved capacity unused, while a medium-priority service is unnecessarily throttled. Later, a high-priority burst may arrive and the fixed slice may still be too small. Another beginner move is one coarse rate limit per application or group. That fails when the real contention happens at the flow and packet level, where many small streams compete and latency builds before a coarse controller notices.
34.ap: BeeQoS separates the job into two layers that work at different speeds. The data plane is powered by eBPF, meaning small programs run inside the operating system's packet path so each packet can be shaped with low overhead. That layer handles fine-grained per-packet action: it can decide how traffic should be paced without sending every decision to a slow external service. Above it, a demand-aware control plane watches real-time flow requirements and reallocates bandwidth as the workload changes. Kubernetes integration gives users an expressive way to state policies and gives the system a natural place to deploy those policies across the cluster. The core move is therefore adaptive priority accounting: keep packet handling fast, keep demand measurement current, and keep policy tied to the cloud system that actually runs the applications.
34.mech: The mechanism begins with policy and traffic. Operators express priority-aware bandwidth rules through the Kubernetes integration, so the system knows which flows or workload classes should be treated as high, medium, or lower priority. Packets then enter the BeeQoS data plane. Because the data plane uses eBPF in the packet path, it can shape traffic at fine granularity without relying on a separate slow queue manager for every packet. At the same time, the control plane observes real-time flow requirements. It is not enough to know that a flow is high priority; the system must also know whether that flow is currently asking for bandwidth, whether lower-priority flows are using capacity that can be reassigned, and whether the cluster has many flows competing at once. The control plane turns those observations into updated bandwidth allocations. Those allocations are then enforced by the data plane, which paces packets according to the current priority and demand state. The output is not a prediction label or a ranked list; it is a running set of bandwidth decisions that determine how quickly packets from different priorities pass through the system. The evaluation evidence in the input says this design remains stable beyond 1,000 flows, improves high- and medium-priority throughput, reduces median latency, lowers deployment overhead, and improves video quality of experience.
34.math: The main mathematics is resource allocation under changing constraints. In plain terms, the system has a limited amount of bandwidth and many claimants. Each claimant has a priority, a current demand, and a cost if it waits too long. The allocation problem is to choose how much service each flow receives while respecting the physical limit of the link and the policy promise attached to priorities. This is an optimization problem, meaning the system must define what counts as a bad allocation, such as unmet high-priority demand, unnecessary delay, or wasted reserved capacity, and repeatedly choose settings that reduce that badness. It also uses control reasoning: measure the current state, compare it with the desired state, adjust the knobs, and repeat as the state changes. Probability enters more lightly through measurement of live demand: recent flow behavior is evidence about what capacity is needed now, but it can be noisy or short-lived. The priority structure is a weighted rule: not every byte has the same urgency, so the system gives different influence to traffic classes. The tradeoff is precision versus overhead. Per-packet shaping gives fine control, but only works if the enforcement path stays cheap enough to run at cloud speed.
34.dots: BeeQoS sits in the conference's efficiency and scalability thread because it asks which work must be handled in full detail and which work can be controlled by compact, repeatable rules. In the repo's efficiency family, it is grouped with systems that preserve the useful decision signal while cutting waste: search systems prune evidence, recommendation systems keep sparse active pieces, graph systems avoid paying for every link, and BeeQoS avoids hand-shaped static rules for every changing flow. It also connects to probability and feedback ideas seen in network and video papers: a system watches recent behavior, treats it as evidence about current capacity pressure, and adjusts before the user-visible experience collapses. The neighboring mathematical idea is selective weighting. Just as ranking and recommendation papers decide which candidates deserve more influence, BeeQoS decides which traffic classes and active demands deserve scarce bandwidth now.
34.ww: The design should work better than a fixed shaper because it matches the two time scales of the problem. Packet forwarding needs immediate action, so BeeQoS puts the enforcement logic in the fast data plane. Demand changes more slowly than individual packet arrivals, so the control plane can spend more time sensing flow requirements and recalculating allocations. This division avoids asking one component to do everything. A static token-bucket style hierarchy can enforce a prewritten budget, but it cannot easily notice that unused high-priority capacity should be reassigned or that a new high-priority burst needs protection. A coarse cloud rate limit can cap traffic, but it cannot express many priority levels with packet-level precision. BeeQoS gains its advantage by making the allocation rule both local enough to act quickly and global enough to see changing demand. The reported throughput, latency, deployment, and video-quality results are exactly the kinds of outcomes this mechanism is meant to improve.
34.po: The payoff is a more practical quality-of-service layer for cloud clusters. According to the input, BeeQoS scales beyond 1,000 flows with stable performance, raises high-priority throughput by 14.6 percent and medium-priority throughput by 36.4 percent, cuts median latency by 72.4 percent, reduces deployment overhead, and improves video quality of experience by 27.3 percent over state-of-practice baselines. In operational terms, that means a cluster can express priority policies, adapt to changing tenants, and enforce bandwidth promises without falling back to static Linux shaping or coarse cloud-native limits. The paper buys finer control while keeping the system deployable in Kubernetes.
34.limits: The abstract leaves several assumptions visible. BeeQoS depends on priorities being correctly specified; if applications mark ordinary traffic as urgent, the allocation rule may protect the wrong flows. It also depends on demand sensing being timely enough that the control plane reacts before congestion has already harmed latency. The evaluation reports 1,000-plus flows and strong gains, but the abstract does not prove behavior under every cluster size, traffic mix, failure mode, or adversarial tenant. Fine per-packet shaping also assumes the eBPF data path remains cheap on the target infrastructure. The paper shows practical improvement over named baselines, but the abstract does not establish hard guarantees for all workloads.

35.bp: A large video site has to decide, many times a day, which few videos should appear in front of a person. The easy goal is watch time: show the videos the person is most likely to keep watching. But a platform is also an ecosystem. If the same familiar channels, creators, or content types keep winning, viewers receive less variety and emerging creators receive fewer chances to be discovered. This paper studies that pressure at the final ordering stage of video recommendation. The target is familiarity bias: the tendency for known content to dominate because the user already has a history with it. The paper's practical aim is not to replace the whole recommender. It tries to make the final ranked list less trapped by familiarity while still preserving the platform goals the abstract names: stable overall watch time, short-term satisfaction, creator exposure, and content diversity.
35.wh: The hard part is that familiar content is not simply bad. A viewer may genuinely enjoy a creator they already know, and a recommendation system should not punish that preference blindly. The problem is that familiarity can become extra evidence on top of preference. Past exposure creates more interactions, more ratings, and more confidence, so the ranking system may learn that known content is safer even when a less familiar video could also satisfy the viewer. That creates a loop: familiar items are shown because they have evidence, and they gain more evidence because they are shown. Novel content and emerging creators stay uncertain because they receive fewer chances. A fix also has to run inside a real serving stack, after other ranking work has already happened. It must be lightweight, work with existing models, and avoid damaging the watch time and satisfaction measures that keep the product usable.
35.naive: A smart beginner might reserve a fixed share of every recommendation list for unfamiliar videos, or subtract the same penalty from every video the user has seen before. That fails because users do not have the same relationship to familiarity. One viewer may repeatedly return to a known creator for good reasons; another may be stuck seeing known material because the system rarely offers alternatives. A flat novelty quota can push weak candidates into the list and hurt satisfaction. A flat penalty can remove videos that are both familiar and genuinely wanted. The abstract says LAFB instead estimates personalized debiasing factors, which means the correction changes with the user and the content rather than treating all familiarity as the same mistake.
35.ap: The central move is to treat familiarity as a measurable pressure in the final ranking, then adjust predicted rating scores by a personalized correction. LAFB, or Learning to Alleviate Familiarity Bias, sits in the post-ranking stage. That means another recommender has already produced candidate videos and predicted how much the user may value them. LAFB does not need to be the main ranking model. It models how familiar a user is with content using both discrete interaction features, such as count-like or category-like signs of prior interaction, and continuous interaction features, such as graded amounts of exposure or engagement. From those features it estimates debiasing factors for that particular user-content pair. The adjusted score then changes the final ordering, reducing the automatic dominance of familiar content while still letting strong familiar recommendations remain when the evidence supports them.
35.mech: The mechanism can be read as a late-stage score repair process. First, the serving system has a set of candidate videos for a user and a predicted rating score for each candidate. That score stands in for expected usefulness under the platform's existing recommendation model. Second, LAFB builds a description of user-content familiarity. The abstract says this description uses discrete and continuous interaction features, so the input is not just a yes-or-no flag for whether the user has seen something like this before. It can represent different shapes and degrees of previous interaction. Third, the method learns a personalized debiasing factor from those familiarity signals. In plain terms, it asks how much of the current score may be inflated by the safety and evidence advantage of familiar material for this user. Fourth, the method applies that factor to the predicted rating score, producing an adjusted score. Fifth, the final list is sorted from these adjusted scores. The output is still a ranked video list, but the list has less pressure toward already familiar content. The abstract reports two kinds of evaluation: large-scale offline tests and online A/B testing inside a real recommendation system. It also says the serving stack compared LAFB with deployable popularity-oriented remedies, which matters because the method was tested against alternatives that could actually run in production.
35.math: The main mathematical object is a score used for ranking. A score compresses many signs about a user and a video into one number so videos can be ordered. The danger is that the number can mix true preference with exposure history. LAFB adds a second mathematical object: a learned correction factor. A factor is a multiplier or adjustment that changes a score without replacing the entire scoring system. The correction is personalized, so it is closer to estimating a local bias for this user-content pair than applying a global rule. The paper also uses feature-based learning. Features are measured clues: some are discrete, meaning they fall into separate buckets or counts; others are continuous, meaning they vary by degree. Learning here means using past interaction evidence to choose how those clues should change the debiasing factor. The ranking idea is then constrained comparison: videos are still compared by scores, but the scores are altered so familiarity does not count as strongly when it mainly reflects prior exposure. The tradeoff is engagement versus discovery, with short-term satisfaction and watch time on one side and novel watch-time share, emerging creator exposure, and content diversity on the other. The math fits because the product decision is comparative and late-stage: a small score adjustment can change which borderline videos become visible.
35.dots: This paper sits where recommendation, ranking, fairness, and probability meet. It is a recommender paper because the object is a user choosing among videos. It is a ranking paper because the final decision is an ordered list, and small changes near the visible cutoff matter. It is a fairness and bias paper because exposure is uneven: emerging creators and less familiar content can lose attention even when they might be valuable. It also has a probability flavor because the original rating prediction is an estimate under uncertainty, and familiarity can make that estimate look safer than it really is. In the repo's broader recommendation family, this is one branch of the shared problem of repairing comparison before selection. Other recommender papers may address missing modalities, long behavior histories, cold starts, or time-aware transfer. LAFB addresses a different surface symptom: the system has too much confidence in what the user already knows.
35.ww: The method should help because it attacks the loop at the place where the loop becomes visible: the final order. Familiar content often has many prior interactions, so the main recommender can treat it as a lower-risk choice. If LAFB can estimate when that advantage is partly familiarity rather than actual added preference, then reducing the score slightly can let nearby unfamiliar candidates rise. This does not require forcing random novelty into the list. It only changes comparisons where the learned factor says familiarity is distorting the score. Personalization is important because the same amount of prior interaction can mean different things for different people. For one viewer, repeated watching may show a stable preference. For another, it may show that the system has narrowed the menu. Running after the main ranking stage also makes the idea deployable: it can adjust outputs from existing models, compare against other post-ranking remedies, and preserve the serving stack. The abstract's online A/B testing and YouTube launch are evidence that the adjustment was practical enough for real traffic, not only an offline score exercise.
35.po: The payoff is a recommender that can make room for discovery without throwing away engagement. The abstract says LAFB increases novel watch-time share, improves exposure for emerging creators, and improves overall content diversity. It also says overall watch time and short-term satisfaction remain stable. That combination is the important result: the method buys a way to reduce familiar-content dominance in the final ranking while keeping the system acceptable to viewers and the platform. The YouTube launch strengthens the practical claim, because it shows the method fit an existing large-scale recommendation pipeline.
35.limits: The abstract does not prove that familiarity is always harmful, only that reducing its dominance improved the reported measures in this setting. The method assumes that interaction features can separate useful familiarity from biased overexposure well enough to guide score adjustment. It also assumes the original predicted rating scores are worth repairing rather than replacing. The reported benefits depend on the chosen metrics: novel watch-time share, emerging creator exposure, diversity, overall watch time, and short-term satisfaction. The abstract does not show long-term user welfare, creator outcomes beyond exposure, effects across all creator groups, or whether the same factors transfer to platforms unlike YouTube.

36.bp: GCAgent starts from a familiar social problem: a group chat is useful only when people keep participating and when the conversation stays manageable. A chat room can be a place for shared interests, quick help, planning, or problem solving, but it can also go quiet, fragment into side topics, or depend on one active person to keep it alive. One-to-one dialogue agents do not solve this by themselves, because a private chat has a single user goal and a clearer turn order. A group has many people, many possible needs, and a stronger risk that an automated voice will interrupt or annoy the room. The paper is trying to make language-model agents act like optional participants and helpers inside that shared space. The goal is not just to answer questions. It is to raise group activity and usefulness by adding agents that can entertain, help with tasks, and be easy for ordinary users to call into the conversation.
36.wh: The hard part is that group conversation is not a longer version of a private conversation. In a one-to-one chat, the system can usually assume that the latest user message is directed at it. In a group chat, a message may be for one person, for everyone, for no one in particular, or for an agent only if someone explicitly asks. The system must decide when silence is better than speaking. It must also decide which kind of agent fits the moment: a playful agent that keeps the room lively, or a utility-oriented agent that answers a question or helps manage the discussion. If every agent responds whenever it can, the chat becomes crowded. If agents wait for perfect instructions, they will not reduce inactivity. The paper therefore faces a coordination problem: keep enough awareness of the dialogue state to add value while preserving the human flow that makes group chat feel natural.
36.naive: A smart beginner might take an existing one-to-one language-model chatbot and invite it into the group. Whenever someone types a question or a quiet period appears, the bot could answer or suggest a topic. That fails because it treats the group as one user with one stable intent. It may answer a remark that was meant for another person, repeat what humans already handled, speak too often, or use a tone that does not match the group. Another simple approach is to require explicit commands for every bot action. That avoids some interruptions, but it keeps the interaction heavy: users must remember how to summon the agent, decide what to ask, and manually manage the bot. The abstract's focus on inactivity, management challenges, dialogue states, agent invocations, and interface plugins shows that neither always-on chatting nor command-only access is enough.
36.ap: The core move is to split the group-chat agent into three connected responsibilities instead of asking one model call to do everything. The Agent Builder handles fit: it customizes agents around user interests, so an agent is not just a generic answer machine. The Dialogue Manager handles timing and coordination: it tracks the current state of the conversation and decides when an agent should be invoked. The Interface Plugins handle friction: they give users three tools that make it easier to interact with agents without turning every action into a carefully written prompt. This structure treats group chat as a shared activity with roles, state, and user-facing controls. Entertainment-oriented agents and utility-oriented agents can then be used for different purposes while still passing through the same management layer. The important idea is controlled participation: agents should be available enough to raise engagement, but constrained enough that they do not take over the room.
36.mech: The mechanism begins with a live group-chat setting and information about the group's interests. That information feeds the Agent Builder, whose job is to create or customize dialogue agents that fit what the users care about. The abstract does not specify the exact customization interface, so the safe claim is that the builder aligns agent behavior with interests rather than leaving every group with the same generic persona. Once agents exist, the Dialogue Manager watches the conversation as a sequence of turns and states. A state is the system's working description of what is happening now: whether the chat is active or quiet, whether a utility need has appeared, and whether an agent invocation would fit the moment. The manager then coordinates agent calls. This is the key gate: before a language model produces a message, another component decides whether the agent should be used and, implicitly, which agent role makes sense. After an agent is invoked, the generated response returns to the group through the interface. The Interface Plugins reduce the cost of controlling the system by providing three distinct tools for interaction. In practical terms, the loop is: observe the group, maintain dialogue state, match the moment to an entertainment or utility agent, invoke the model when appropriate, send the response through a low-friction interface, and continue observing how the conversation changes.
36.math: This paper is mostly a system design and deployment paper, not a paper claiming a new mathematical method. Still, several mathematical ideas sit underneath the design. The first is sequence state: a conversation is an ordered record, and the meaning of a message depends on what came before it. A dialogue manager must compress recent turns into a useful description of the current situation, because it cannot treat every past sentence as equally important forever. The second idea is decision under uncertainty. The system must choose whether to call an agent even though it cannot perfectly know user intent, annoyance, or future engagement. That choice is a scoring problem in plain language: estimate whether speaking now is likely to help more than silence. The third idea is matching. Agent Builder tries to align agents with user interests, which means comparing a group's preferences or topics with possible agent behaviors. The fourth idea is optimization in the everyday sense of adjusting a designed process to reduce what counts as wrong: too much inactivity, too much friction, badly timed agent messages, or poor user preference. The reported average score, preference comparison with the base model, and message-volume increase are measurements of whether those design choices moved the system in the desired direction.
36.dots: GCAgent belongs with the conference's broader work on language-model agents and tool use because it turns a model from a private responder into a participant in a larger activity. It is close to multi-agent workflow papers such as lesson-plan generation, where roles are separated so that different agent voices contribute different kinds of work. It is also close to production agent papers in shopping or search, because the central issue is not only text quality but orchestration: when should the system act, which component should act, and how much cost or friction should the user feel? The paper also connects to sequence modeling, because group conversation unfolds over time, and to interface research, because usefulness depends on how easily people can invite, steer, or ignore the agents. Its theme, LLM group chat, is therefore a special case of a wider pattern: language models become more useful when wrapped in controls that decide role, timing, and user access.
36.ww: The system should improve over the naive one-bot approach because it separates fit, timing, and access. Customization helps because a group is more likely to accept an agent whose topics and tone match its interests. Dialogue management helps because the system does not have to respond to every possible opening; it can coordinate invocations around the current state of the chat. That matters in group settings where a useful message at the wrong time can still be harmful. Interface plugins help because the burden of using the agent is moved away from perfect prompting. Users can engage through tools designed for the chat setting, which lowers the barrier to occasional use. The deployment result gives practical support for this logic: over 350 days, message volume increased by 28.80 percent, which is the kind of behavioral outcome the system was built to change. The preference result over the base model also suggests that the surrounding coordination system adds value beyond the underlying language model alone, though the margin reported is modest.
36.po: The payoff is a practical blueprint for moving dialogue agents from one-party chats into multi-party group scenarios. The paper reports an average score of 4.68 across criteria, a 51.04 percent preference rate compared with the base model, and a 28.80 percent message-volume increase during real-world deployments over 350 days. Those numbers matter because the target problem is not only answer correctness; it is group activity and engagement. The system buys a way to add entertainment and utility agents to social chats while giving the platform a management layer for customization, state tracking, invocation, and user-facing controls.
36.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The dialogue manager must read enough context to decide when an agent is welcome, but the abstract does not prove that it understands every social cue or avoids all awkward interruptions. Agent customization assumes user interests are available, stable enough, and safe to reflect back into agent behavior. Higher message volume is useful only if the added messages are valuable rather than noise. The 51.04 percent preference over the base model is positive but close, so it should not be read as overwhelming dominance. The abstract also gives system modules and deployment outcomes, but not enough detail to judge privacy handling, moderation failures, long-term user fatigue, or performance across very different group cultures.

37.bp: Many web and scientific datasets are networks: people linked to people, papers linked by citations, products linked by co-purchase, or accounts linked by transactions. A graph foundation model is meant to be a reusable learner for many such networks, instead of a separate hand-built model for each one. The difficulty is that links do not always mean the same thing. In some networks, connected things tend to resemble each other; friends may share interests, and papers may cite similar papers. In other networks, links often join different things; a buyer connects to a seller, or a paper cites work from another area. This paper serves the need for one graph learner that can handle both cases. Its starting point is finer than the usual question, "Are neighboring nodes similar?" It asks whether each individual feature follows the link pattern in its own way.
37.wh: The hard part is that a graph link is only a clue, not a guarantee. If connected nodes are usually similar, then borrowing information from neighbors is helpful. If connected nodes are usually different, the same borrowing can damage the prediction because it mixes unlike things as if they were alike. Existing graph foundation models, according to the abstract, usually work under the similar-neighbor assumption, so they are poorly prepared for networks where many useful links cross between different kinds of nodes. The problem is harder for a reusable model than for a custom graph model because one model must adapt to many unseen graphs with different structures, features, and tasks. The abstract also says even mostly similar-neighbor graphs contain limited but useful different-neighbor information. A whole-node label like "similar" or "different" is therefore too crude: one feature may match neighbors while another feature contrasts with them.
37.naive: A smart beginner would first let every node average or collect information from its neighbors, because the graph says those neighbors matter. That works when links usually join similar nodes, but it fails when a neighbor is informative because it is different. Averaging a buyer with sellers, or one class of node with an opposing class, can erase the very pattern the link was meant to reveal. A second beginner answer is to decide that an entire graph, or an entire node, is either similar-neighbor or different-neighbor and then choose one rule. The abstract argues that this is still too rough, because the split can happen feature by feature. Treating all features together hides the small, useful exceptions.
37.ap: The core idea is to let the graph structure sort the features before the model decides how to use them. A feature is one measured column attached to a node, such as a property, count, category signal, or learned numeric description. The paper's claim is that similarity and difference are not only properties of whole nodes; they can appear separately inside these feature columns. Topology-aware feature sorting means looking at how a feature behaves across the local links around a node: does this feature tend to agree with connected nodes, or does it tend to differ from them? The model then uses a dual-channel graph neural network, meaning two coordinated routes for passing information through the graph. One route can handle features whose neighbor agreement is useful, while the other can preserve or use features whose neighbor disagreement is useful. The output is a unified graph foundation model for both link patterns.
37.mech: The mechanism starts with a graph: nodes, links, and a table of node features. The first job is not to predict immediately, but to inspect how each feature relates to the local topology, meaning the pattern of nearby links. For a given feature dimension, the method can compare a node's value with the values carried by its linked neighbors. If linked nodes tend to have nearby values for that feature, the feature behaves like a similar-neighbor clue. If linked nodes tend to have contrasting values, the feature behaves like a different-neighbor clue. The sorting step orders or groups features according to that local graph behavior, so the model does not have to treat the whole node description as one undivided bundle. Next, the dual-channel network processes the sorted information. In the similar-neighbor channel, evidence from linked nodes can be blended because agreement across links is meaningful. In the different-neighbor channel, the model must keep track of contrast rather than simple sameness, because the useful signal may be that a node connects to unlike neighbors. The two channels then combine feature information with structural information. What comes out is a node or graph representation usable for varying downstream tasks, while the same model can adapt to homophilic, heterophilic, and mixed graphs.
37.math: The mathematical object is a graph with a feature matrix. A graph is a map of items and relationships; a feature matrix is a table where each row describes one item and each column records one kind of signal. Classic graph neural networks use a message-passing rule: each node updates its description by receiving numbers from its neighbors and mixing them with its own numbers. That rule quietly assumes that neighbor information should usually be smoothed together. Smoothing means reducing local differences by averaging or blending nearby values. This paper's mathematical move is to decide when smoothing is the wrong operation. It measures feature-level agreement with topology: for each column, the relevant question is whether linked nodes show similar or contrasting values. Sorting is then a structured reordering of the feature columns according to that measured relation. The dual-channel design is a decomposition: split one mixed signal bundle into two routes whose rules can fit different link meanings. The tradeoff is local evidence versus neighbor evidence. Too much neighbor mixing can erase differences; too little can waste the graph. Feature-level sorting tries to spend neighbor sharing only where the graph says it helps.
37.dots: This paper belongs to the graph learning and mining family because it treats links as evidence that must be moved carefully. It connects to the repo's network concept: the common question is how far a clue should travel, how much it should change on the way, and when a connection misleads. Compared with graph retrieval, graph anomaly detection, or microservice forecasting papers, the surface task is different, but the deeper pressure is the same: isolated records are thin, while connected records can help only if the meaning of the connection is understood. It also connects to similarity and learning. Similarity is not taken as a single global fact; it is measured at the feature level. Learning enters because the model must reuse this sorting-and-routing behavior across unseen graphs, rather than being tuned for one fixed network. The broader conference pattern is adaptation under mixed structure.
37.ww: The approach should work because it corrects the main false assumption in the beginner method. Neighbor information is not always bad on different-neighbor graphs; it is bad when the model uses the wrong operation on it. If a feature tends to match across links, blending it with neighbors can strengthen a weak local signal. If a feature tends to differ across links, the contrast itself can be informative, but plain blending would wash it away. By sorting features according to their topological behavior, the model gives each kind of signal a better route. This also explains why the method may help even on graphs that are mostly similar-neighbor. The abstract says those graphs still contain limited but informative heterophilic information, so a model that assumes total sameness leaves useful evidence unused. The universal-model claim depends on this finer granularity: instead of switching whole models for whole graph types, the same architecture can adjust how individual feature dimensions interact with links.
37.po: The payoff is a graph foundation model that is less tied to one link meaning. The abstract claims TFSGFM enables unified modeling of both feature and structure and supports universal modeling on homophilic and heterophilic graphs. In practical terms, it buys a reusable way to learn from networks where connected items may be similar in some properties and different in others. That matters for unseen graphs because the model cannot assume in advance that every new network follows the same neighbor rule. The reported extensive experiments, though truncated in the input, are presented as evidence that this feature-level view improves adaptation across graph types.
37.limits: The input abstract is truncated, so the exact datasets, metrics, baselines, and experimental results are not available here. The method assumes that local link patterns reveal whether a feature should be treated as agreement-based or contrast-based; noisy links or poorly measured features could make the sorting unreliable. It also assumes two channels are enough to capture the important split between similar-neighbor and different-neighbor behavior. The abstract does not prove how the model behaves when feature meanings change across domains, when tasks require information absent from topology, or when links are adversarial, accidental, or too sparse to judge feature-level patterns.

38.bp: Modern web applications are often built from many small services that call one another. A user request may pass through login, search, payment, storage, caching, and message queues before the page or API response comes back. A trace is the recorded path of that request: which service handled it, when each step started, how long it took, and where errors appeared. Engineers use traces to understand normal behavior, detect unusual behavior, and diagnose faults. The paper asks whether large language models, which are text models trained to follow written instructions and produce written answers, can help with this operational work. The need comes before the model: industrial microservice systems are too tangled for every trace question to be handled by manual inspection or by narrow tools built for one task. TraceLLM treats trace analysis as a set of instruction-and-response problems so a model can answer many trace questions through a more flexible interface.
38.wh: The hard part is that a trace is not just a log line. It is a small story about cause, timing, dependency, and abnormal behavior across many services.
